reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service with 200,000 active users. A bad change takes 10 minutes to detect. Option 1 releases everything to all users at once; option 2 releases each change to 1% of users first (a canary) and widens only if the canary is healthy. The figures are illustrative.

Derivation: a bad change released to everyone affects 200,000 users × 10 minutes = 2,000,000 user-minutes before detection. Released to a 1% canary, it affects 2,000 users × 10 minutes = 20,000 user-minutes, a hundredth of the harm. If 40 changes ship as one batch and the release fails, finding the culprit by halving the batch takes up to 6 rounds, because 2^5 = 32 < 40 ≤ 64 = 2^6; a change shipped alone has one suspect.

Independent check: the SRE book reports that roughly 70% of outages at Google come from changes to a live system and recommends three practices: progressive rollouts, quick and accurate detection, and safe rollback. Each one reduces a term in the harm calculation above: the users exposed, the minutes to detect and the minutes to undo.

Misconception to reject: 'more approvers make a change safer.' DORA's research found no evidence that a more formal external review process was associated with lower change failure rates, while heavier approval slowed delivery and produced larger, less frequent releases. DORA recommends peer review recorded in the delivery platform, plus automated testing and monitoring.
Change one factor: automated canary analysis cuts detection from 10 minutes to 2. The full-release harm falls to 200,000 × 2 = 400,000 user-minutes and the canary harm to 2,000 × 2 = 4,000.

Source and limits: the 70% figure and the three practices come from chapter 1 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book: https://sre.google/sre-book/introduction/. The approval findings come from DORA's capability page on streamlining change approval: https://dora.dev/capabilities/streamlining-change-approval/. Regulated environments may still require a recorded approval; DORA suggests meeting it through peer review in the normal workflow.

reasoningSteps: Assume a fictional constant total traffic rate of 1,000 requests per second, a 5% candidate share and a candidate-only defect rate of 20%. Assume control has no additional defect and there is no spillover.
The modeled additional failures per second are 1,000 times 0.05 times 0.20 = 10. A 120-second exposure produces 1,200 additional failures.
At 100% exposure for the same 120 seconds, the model gives 24,000 failures. But a 5% canary left for 3,000 seconds gives 30,000: smaller share alone does not guarantee lower total impact.
This expected-count model assumes stable routing, load and defect rate. It does not bound data loss, privacy harm or shared-dependency damage, and does not justify spending any real error budget.

reasoningSteps: The SRE Workbook warns that shared dependencies can make canary and control fail together; relative comparison must be complemented by absolute health measures.
In a fictional review, candidate and control each have 100 errors in 1,000 requests: their rates match at 10%. A difference-only rule reports no degradation.

For a fictional canary beginning at minute 30 and evaluated at minute 60, use the declared half-open interval [30,60). Synthetic error events at minutes 10,20,35,45 yield two in-window errors, not four.
